“That’s the casting that would sell the idea. It’s interesting because when we made the first one there was also a rush to get it out; editors slept in the cutting room on shifts. This is a weird thing, like they want it to come out and tank.”
![Randy Quaid has railed against the forthcoming ‘Days of Thunder’ film](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/30/16/18/Randy-Quaid.png)
In a separate post, Quaid again advocated for Kidman’s casting while railing against Hathaway and Cruise, writing: “We need Nicole back. Don’t be a p***y, @TomCruise. You need the original girl. It’s not personal; it’s filmmaking. Anne isn’t sexy, because and if you haven’t noticed, she’s pregnant.”
And in yet another post, he wrote: “If I were in control of production, a real sequel worth watching for DAYS OF THUNDER would be seeing Tom and Nicole together on screen again. We don’t need a new girl; we need a new race car!”
The Independent has contacted representatives for Cruise and Hathaway for comment.
Hathaway is one of the most in-demand stars in Hollywood, with four films out already this year and another — Verity, the latest film adaptation from author Colleen Hoover — slated for an October release.
![Tom Cruise and Anne Hathaway are teaming up for a 'Days of Thunder' follow up film](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/30/16/01M17JKWZ805EMCPCZ3M38DBHZ.jpg)
An Oscar winner for the 2012 film adaptation of Les Misérables, Hathaway is also pregnant with her third child. She confirmed in the announcement for the Days of Thunder sequel that she’ll give birth before filming commences.
Hathaway and Cruise will film the sequel nearly 40 years after the original movie was released. The new film is slated for a June 2028 release.
According to Variety, Cruise will reprise his role from the first film as Cole Trickle. Hathaway will play a racecar team owner and engineer. Jonathan Levine will direct, and Cruise will produce alongside Jerry Bruckheimer and Tommy Harper.
In addition to Cruise, the original Days of Thunder starred Kidman, Quaid, Robert Duvall and John C. Reilly. It is not yet clear whether any of the original cast will return for the follow up. Duvall died earlier this year.
summary: Original Days of Thunder star Randy Quaid criticized the casting of Anne Hathaway in the upcoming sequel on social media. Quaid argued that Tom Cruise should reunite with his original co-star, Nicole Kidman, instead of Hathaway. Cruise and Hathaway are set to star in the follow-up film directed by Jonathan Levine, scheduled for a June 2028 release.
key_points: Randy Quaid publicly criticized Anne Hathaway's casting in the Days of Thunder sequel on X.
Quaid advocated for Nicole Kidman to return as Tom Cruise's love interest instead of Hathaway.
Tom Cruise will reprise his role as Cole Trickle, while Hathaway will play a racecar team owner and engineer.
The sequel is directed by Jonathan Levine and slated for a June 2028 release.

title: Vigil recaptures its mojo in the Arctic
author: Benji Wilson
content:
![Rose Leslie and Suranne Jones head to the Arctic for the third series of the BBC thriller](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/tv/2026/08/27/TELEMMGLPICT000499698708_17878301203520_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqMNWpgD2PZIvlOBIGuRStEyqVm7pDLexZy36ab3xAREw.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Rose Leslie and Suranne Jones head to the Arctic for the third series of the BBC thriller](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/tv/2026/08/27/TELEMMGLPICT000499698708_17878301203520_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqMNWpgD2PZIvlOBIGuRStEyqVm7pDLexZy36ab3xAREw.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The first series of Vigil (BBC One) was set on a submarine and was very good, precisely because it was set on a submarine. A disparate group of sailors cooped up for months, going loco and killing each other – what’s not to like? The second series, two years later, widened its horizons and lost its mojo. It was all about drones and, true to its subject, felt like it went on a bit. For series three, therefore, Tom Edge, the writer, has tried to replicate the sardine-can sense of isolation and dread from series one by transplanting the whole thing to remotest Svalbard, Norway.
Once again, we get the dynamic duo of Amy Silva (Suranne Jones) and Kirsten Longacre (Rose Leslie), who in episode one are summoned to a remote Arctic research station after a tough nut in a covert British special forces mission is shot dead. Needless to say, this one goes right to the very top, as conspiracy thrillers always do. (As an aside, I long for a thriller whose big reveal is that it doesn’t go to the very top, and is just a miscreant doing something silly at the very bottom that is solved by a junior detective in 25 minutes and doesn’t involve bald men in navy suits barking: “Just get it done!” into secure phones).
![tmg.video.placeholder.alt t2GzDAN1q2A](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/t2GzDAN1q2A/maxresdefault.jpg) 
The plus points of an Arctic setting are the aforementioned stir-craziness and the fact that everyone has to carry a high-powered rifle around in case they bump into a polar bear. All of the ingredients for seemingly random killings are right there. The downside is that screenwriters have noticed this already: both 2015’s Fortitude and 2024’s True Detective: Night Country used strange happenings at distant research stations conducting controversial environmental studies as their jumping-off points.
Not that you’d ever get bored of glaciers and long horizons, but it does mean that Vigil series three has to work for exciting incidents. The show throws Russians, Chinese, spies, special forces, eco-terrorists, the fossil-fuel disaster and the completely impossible task of politicians trying to work through all of the above into the mix.
The task facing the producers of a drama like this one is to tip-toe down the tightrope of implausibility while holding the balancing pole of the feasible. Vigil gets it just about right, asking pertinent questions about the climate emergency without lecturing, while still allowing itself the luxury of imagining that someone is coming to fix things.
![The show manages to  tip-toe down the tightrope of implausibility](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/tv/2026/08/27/TELEMMGLPICT000499024504_17878299632870_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
But it does suffer from the old X-Files problem of “trust no one”, It’s one thing for Silva and Longacre to be asking themselves who they can trust (answer: no one), but there’s the further issue of who the viewer can trust. We know now in conspiracy thrillers that the nameless nice guys are most often the wrong’uns, but we still need to feel that the writers have interests at heart other than just getting us to the next episode.
On this count, Vigil broadly succeeds, because its central characters are credible and well played. You stick with the show, as daft as it sometimes gets, because you want to stick with its leading ladies. Ultimately, in a world full of liars, they’re just trying to work out what’s the right thing to do and how to do it. Buy that, and you’ll follow them all the way to Svalbard and back.
Vigil is on BBC One at 9pm on Sunday, Aug 30, and BBC iPlayer
summary: The third series of the BBC thriller Vigil relocates its action to a remote Arctic research station in Svalbard, Norway, aiming to recapture the isolated atmosphere of the first season. Detectives Amy Silva and Kirsten Longacre return to investigate the murder of a British special forces member in a plot involving international espionage and environmental issues. Despite familiar conspiracy tropes, the show succeeds largely due to the credible and well-played performances of its leading actresses.
key_points: Series three of Vigil is set in remotest Svalbard, Norway, to replicate the isolated atmosphere of the first season.
Suranne Jones and Rose Leslie return as dynamic duo Amy Silva and Kirsten Longacre.
The plot begins with the murder of a covert British special forces operative at an Arctic research station.
The narrative incorporates complex elements including international spies, eco-terrorists, and the climate emergency.
The show maintains viewer engagement primarily through the credible performances of its central characters.

title: Reading Festival: Messy singer Lola Young makes surprise final day appearance
author: Adam Goldsmith
content:
![Singer Lola Young is pictured on stage at the Reading music festival. She is smiling while holding a microphone. She is wearing a black top with a tartan trim.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/699/cpsprodpb/0fc2/live/5d0d2160-a495-11f1-8395-fb1eae51ae18.jpg)
- Published
Fans at the final day of Reading Festival were treated to a surprise set from singer Lola Young.
"I am backstage, the cat is out of the bag and I am going to be performing so see you... at the Grid stage," she teased on Instagram, before treating fans to hits including number one single Messy and One Thing.
Her performance marks the latest step in a return to the spotlight after she had to cancel a string of shows last year following an on-stage collapse in September.
Young also pulled out of the 2025 Reading festival due to a scheduling clash.
The weekend festival concludes on Sunday with a line-up including performances by drum and bass duo Chase & Status, and Florence + The Machine.
After Charli XCX ushered in her own new era with an electrifying set following her latest release Music, Fashion, Film, Young's return was welcomed by festival-goers in Reading on Sunday.
Young had cancelled her scheduled appearance at Reading Festival last year due to an "unavoidable scheduling conflict".
A month later, Young dropped her microphone, collapsed backwards and had to be helped off stage in front of a festival crowd in New York.
A few days later, she cancelled all shows "for the foreseeable future".
"I really hope you'll give me a second chance once I've had some time to work on myself and come back stronger," she posted in a message to fans at the time.
Young has sought treatment for drug dependency and told the Guardian, external in 2025 that addiction had dogged her for "a long time".
The pop star has since returned to performing with a small run of shows in the UK, starting with a London gig in March.
"It felt so right being back on stage," she wrote on social media shortly after, but said: "As tempting as it is to jump on a big tour I'm going to continue taking things slowly despite feeling so ready to perform more."
Before touching down in Reading, Young performed at the Electric Picnic Festival in the Republic of Ireland on Saturday.
Although she has returned to performing and released reflective single From Down Here in May this year, fans are still awaiting a fourth album.
Reading Festival winds down on Sunday night with a star-studded cast including indie icon Florence and the Machine, R&B hit-maker Loyle Carner, and Irish rap group Kneecap.
The festival's other site in Leeds, meanwhile, closes after performances from singer-songwriter Raye and multi award-winning rapper Dave on Sunday night.
![Lola Young on stage in green trousers and a black top](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/998/cpsprodpb/61bb/live/f61c1e00-a49b-11f1-837c-8514728b4183.jpg)
- ![A black and white photo of Charli XCX leaning against a wall as she sings into a microphone. There is a bright white wall behind her which silhouettes her body.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/86ea/live/35df52c0-a32d-11f1-8e46-c39d9fc92d9e.jpg)
  - Published5 March
 ![Lola young on stage playing an acoustic guitar and singing into a microphone](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/e0f0/live/87b385e0-186c-11f1-8f1d-d7bdb1ea156f.jpg)
  - Published2 days ago
 ![Crowds of festival-goers wave their hands in the air at Leeds Festival. There a few people in the crowd raised up by sitting on the shoulders of other people.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/5d84/live/c30d5820-a249-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
summary: Singer Lola Young made a surprise appearance on the final day of the Reading Festival, performing hits including her number one single Messy on the Grid stage. This performance marks a continuation of her return to the spotlight after she cancelled shows last year following an on-stage collapse and treatment for drug dependency. Young previously missed out on festival appearances due to scheduling clashes and health reasons, but she has recently begun a gradual return to live performing.
key_points: Lola Young delivered a surprise set on the final day of the Reading Festival.
She performed hits like Messy and One Thing on the Grid stage.
The performance is part of her gradual return to the stage following an on-stage collapse and treatment for drug dependency last year.
Prior to Reading, she performed at the Electric Picnic Festival in Ireland.

title: Dame Meera Syal reveals she was sexually assaulted in her 20s
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
![Meera Syal](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/30/TELEMMGLPICT000488196045_17880985246050_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwauLYewjGO21NF-o1gxbkUI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Meera Syal](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/30/TELEMMGLPICT000488196045_17880985246050_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwauLYewjGO21NF-o1gxbkUI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Dame Meera Syal has said she was sexually assaulted in her 20s, an experience she said had “completely changed my life”.
The 65-year-old actress rose to fame after co-creating and starring in the hit sketch comedy series Goodness Gracious Me, and later appearing in its spin-off The Kumars at No 42.
She has now spoken publicly about being attacked by an older man she thought she could trust until he tried to rape her.
The sexual assault, which happened in the 1980s, was never reported because Dame Meera could not bear the thought of putting her parents through a criminal trial. She told no one at the time.
Speaking to The Times, she said: “This is the first time I’ve spoken about this publicly. It completely changed my life and the direction of my career. I could have given up, but instead I sought out a group of South Asian writers.
“They encouraged me to write more, they found me a place to live, they healed me and awakened me politically.”
Writing strong female characters
Years later, she opened up to a group of friends and learnt that many of them had endured something similar.
Dame Meera said the assault led her to write the strong female characters that have featured in the acclaimed BBC sketch show and other comedy shows that changed her life.
Speaking about the sitcom Goodness Gracious Me, in which her husband, Sanjeev Bhaskar, also starred, she said: “It was a golden age of sketch comedy, alternative comedy and Cool Britannia. There was a real embracing of multicultural Britain. How times have changed.”
Dame Meera said the current political climate is giving her a “horrible sense of deja vu” specifically around immigration. She described how, when growing up, the initials of the far-Right National Front party were painted on her house.
She added: “Some people who feel hard done by need to be listened to, but their frustration is being weaponised and exploited by certain public figures against immigrants.”
Despite her decades-long career, Dame Meera said she does not “glide in and out of jobs” and believes “there still aren’t that many good roles for older women”. Speaking about what her dream role would be, she said: “A badass godmother, head of a clan or a crime syndicate.
“If you had met some of the badass aunties I have met you would know they could run that ship without blinking. And she would be called something you wouldn’t expect, like Sweetie Auntie.”
summary: Dame Meera Syal has publicly revealed for the first time that she was sexually assaulted by an older man in the 1980s when she was in her 20s. She did not report the attack at the time to spare her parents a criminal trial, but the experience ultimately shaped her career and inspired her to write strong female characters. In a recent interview, she also discussed her decades-long acting career, the political climate surrounding immigration, and the scarcity of good roles for older women.
key_points: Dame Meera Syal revealed she was sexually assaulted in her 20s by an older man she thought she could trust.
The 1980s assault was never reported because she did not want to put her parents through a criminal trial.
The experience influenced the direction of her career and inspired her to write strong female characters.
She expressed concern that the current political climate regarding immigration creates a sense of deja vu.
She noted that a lack of good roles for older women persists in the industry.

title: Dolly, inc: How the Queen of Country built her business empire
author: James Hall
content:
![American singer and songwriter Dolly Parton poses for a portrait at Dollywood on October 24, 1988 in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499593342_178774882943617_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqbVGIJc7U-PZBMr9f92rSpGwWMIa6ROzpVxfgVoPIevI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![American singer and songwriter Dolly Parton poses for a portrait at Dollywood on October 24, 1988 in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499593342_178774882943617_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqbVGIJc7U-PZBMr9f92rSpGwWMIa6ROzpVxfgVoPIevI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Dolly Parton, who has died aged 80, will be remembered best for her music. But the country star also ran an astonishing business and entertainment empire that took in everything from theme parks and hit films to clothing for dogs. While most of us were tumbling out of bed and stumbling to the kitchen of a morning, the indefatigable Parton was no doubt already up to keep a close eye on the myriad enterprises that made up Dolly, inc.
“I work my butt off,” the 9 to 5 hitmaker told Bloomberg in a 2024 interview. And her entrepreneurial flair was not restricted to selling rollercoaster rides or rhinestone-encrusted “stuff”. Parton was a trailblazer when it came to owning the rights to her own music and, perhaps incongruously for a musician, helping scientists develop a Covid vaccine during the 2020 pandemic. It’s little wonder that Parton’s net worth has been valued at between $440m and $650m (£340m to £485m).
Parton’s best known business venture is Dollywood, the 160-acre theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, where a two-day adult ticket starts at $125 (£95). Opened in 1986, Dollywood offers visitors more than 50 rides, ranging from the Dollywood Express – a coal-fired steam train that takes people on a five-mile trip through the foothills of the Great Smoky Mountains – to the Tennessee Tornado – a 70mph big dipper. Dollywood also houses theatres, blacksmithery and glass-blowing workshops, and the Dolly Parton Experience, a multi-building tribute to the singer that includes the “Behind the Seams” exhibition about her clothing.
![Photo of COUNTRY & WESTERN and DOLLYWOOD and Dolly PARTON and COUNTRY](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499593344_178774882920215_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqBmo3ZBPOSwC7GqRZsuXAwCTc4m2O3CKB7TalllG6rcY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Also under the Dollywood umbrella sit the Splash Country water park, a horse-based show called Dolly Parton’s Stampede Dinner Attraction and two Dollywood spa resorts. At one of these resorts you can stay in the lavishly upholstered “Gypsy Wagon” tour bus that transported Parton for 360,000 miles across North America between 2008 and 2022. The bus comes with a bath, a wig cabinet, a full-size fridge and hand-painted murals on the walls (a two-night-minimum stay for two people starts at $10,000 (£7,500), with profit going to The Dollywood Foundation). In September, Dolly Parton’s SongTeller Hotel is opening in Nashville. The 245-room hotel, which also contains two live music venues, is her “love letter to the city”, she said.
![In September, Dolly Parton's SongTeller Hotel is due to open in Nashville](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/music/2026/08/28/TELEMMGLPICT000499800537_17879120657880_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
As with most of Parton’s business enterprises, Dollywood is run as a joint venture with a large corporation. In this case it’s Herschend Family Entertainment, the theme park behemoth that also owns the Harlem Globetrotters basketball team. Describing Dollywood earlier this year in a statement to celebrate it being voted America’s favourite theme park by the National Amusement Park Historical Association (above the likes of Disneyland), Herschend said the place “isn’t just a theme park. It’s a love letter to East Tennessee”. Its three million visitors a year clearly agree.
Then there are the TV and film successes. Parton’s production company Sandollar was behind the 1991 Steve Martin hit film Father of the Bride (which grossed $89m at the box office on a $20m budget) and the hugely popular TV show Buffy the Vampire Slayer starring Sarah Michelle Gellar (and also the Buffy spinoff series, Angel). Sandollar was another joint venture, this time with Parton’s former manager Sandy Gallin. The company has gone through various iterations and is now called Dixie Pixie Productions.
Parton’s business ventures wouldn’t have been complete without some high kitsch. In 2022 she launched Doggy Parton, a clothing and accessories line for pooches that included mini cowboy hats, wigs and gingham dresses “with a little Dolly flair”. She also wrote a series of picture books, including a number about a French Bulldog called Billy the Kid. Food featured heavily in her business interests too: she had ranges of branded frozen meals, desserts and baking products. A single box of her sweet cornbread and muffin mix, launched in conjunction with food company Duncan Hines, costs $2.87 at Walmart. The pink packet is dominated by a portrait of Parton – her voluminous golden locks take up almost as much space as the picture of the similarly coloured cornbread.
!['A little Dolly flair': Doggy Parton is a clothing and accessories line for dogs](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499594252_17877488282063_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqAHSO9YcRn5Jrj-vTPE9vj4pXWSGeG3wfTcFmoZLWsNI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
![Dolly Parton Duncan Hines food products](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499594372_17877488269581_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqRo0U4xU-30oDveS4pXV-Vv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Parton readily admitted that her strengths lay in songwriting and performing, so her trick was to cede business decisions to experts. “I just try to put people that are smarter than me in all the right places, and then I go on about my business,” she told Bloomberg. “I’m more of the creative force. I try to find the best people, and I try to trust them to do what they say they can do. Then I have people looking out after all of them.”
One area where she was consistently ruthless was around her songwriting royalties. Parton owned the publishing copyright for nearly all her song catalogue. This stemmed from a strategically smart decision she made back in 1966, aged just 20. When her music publishing contract with a company called Combine Music expired, Parton and her musician uncle Bill Owens founded their own company called Owe-Par Publishing, which meant they could keep the copyright for their songs. Crucially, Parton had a controlling share in Owe-Par. Such deals are increasingly commonplace in music today but back then they were almost unheard of. Over her career Parton estimated she’d written close to 3,000 songs.
As well as writing tracks for herself, her songs were covered by other artists including Tina Turner (1974’s There’ll Always Be Music) and Emmylou Harris (To Daddy, 1977). And with Parton’s own catalogue including Jolene and 9 to 5 (a combined 1.6 billion Spotify streams and counting), the royalties rolled in. Nowhere was this more apparent with I Will Always Love You, which Parton wrote and recorded in 1973.
A hit for Parton in its own right, I Will Always Love You piqued the interest of Elvis Presley, who wanted to cover it in 1974. However it came with a catch: Presley’s manager Colonel Tom Parker told Parton that she’d have to sign over half the publishing rights to Elvis. The steely Parton refused, crying all night that she’d turned down The King. But vindication came when Whitney Houston’s 1992 power-ballad version of the song, from the film The Bodyguard, was number one for 14 weeks in the US and 10 weeks in the UK.
Parton made a reported $20m (£15m) in royalties from Houston’s hit. “When Whitney’s [version] came out, I made enough money to buy Graceland,” Parton wryly told country-music TV channel CMT. According to Business Insider, Parton’s music catalogue earned her royalties of $6 to $8m a year. Taylor Swift is one of the artists who walked through the gate that Parton kicked open when it comes to owning the publishing rights to her songs.
But Dolly, inc wasn’t just about making money. It was about giving it away, too. We tend to equate philanthropy with virtue-signalling in this country. But it’s seen differently in America – and, boy, did Parton make a difference through The Dollywood Foundation, which is funded from her profits.
Her Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library mails one book a month to millions of children around the world from the day they’re born until they’re 5. One in seven children under the age of 5 in the US now receives a monthly book. In 2008, the scheme launched in the UK, where six million books have since been distributed. The fact that Parton launched the Library in honour of her father, who could neither read nor write, adds to its poignancy. Elsewhere, Parton has regularly donated millions of dollars to hospitals and victims of natural disasters, as well as campaigning to preserve the bald eagle when its status was threatened. Some profits from Doggy Parton went to a pet rescue centre. But perhaps Parton’s most notable contribution to public life came during the Covid pandemic.
When Covid struck, Parton donated $1m towards research at Vanderbilt University Medical Centre in Nashville. The donation helped fund the early stages of development of the Moderna vaccine. In March 2021, Parton became one of the first people to be vaccinated with a Moderna shot. “Dolly gets a dose of her own medicine,” she wrote on social media. Before she was injected she sang an adapted version of Jolene: “Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine… I’m begging you, please don’t hesitate / Vaccine, vaccine… Because once you’re dead, then that’s a bit too late.” The following month, the UK government bought 17 million doses of Moderna, enough to vaccinate 8.5 million people.
![Dolly Parton receives a vaccination against the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, Tennessee](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000252360260_178774882852822_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqwtUT54c80eKHJHMfvK9NIl5NUcTKNHKqy85KLqtvPLE.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Dame Kate Bingham, who chaired the UK Vaccine Taskforce, is in little doubt about the role that Parton played. “Dolly Parton’s donation to Vanderbilt helped fund the early immunology work that confirmed the Moderna vaccine produced a protective immune response – a vital step in the discovery of one of the Covid vaccines that ended the pandemic,” Bingham tells me. “Her timely investment in discovery research paid huge dividends for people all over the world. Leadership in science comes in many forms, not just from the lab bench.”
Parton’s cup of ambition knew no bounds.
summary: Dolly Parton built an extensive business and entertainment empire alongside her legendary music career, encompassing theme parks, production companies, hotels, and various consumer products. She was a trailblazer in retaining her music publishing rights, generating millions in royalties while refusing unfavorable deals like Elvis Presley's offer. Furthermore, Parton used her wealth for extensive philanthropy, funding literacy programs, natural disaster relief, and even contributing to early Covid-19 vaccine research.
key_points: Parton co-founded Owe-Par Publishing in 1966 to maintain a controlling share of her music copyrights, earning millions annually in royalties.
Her best-known venture is the 160-acre Dollywood theme park in Tennessee, operated as a joint venture with Herschend Family Entertainment.
Her production company, Sandollar (now Dixie Pixie Productions), worked on successful films and television shows like Father of the Bride and Buffy the Vampire Slayer.
Through The Dollywood Foundation, she established the Imagination Library, which mails free books monthly to millions of children worldwide.
Parton donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center to support early research for the Moderna Covid-19 vaccine.

title: Bill Maher makes sour comment about Dolly Parton’s death
author: Roisin O'Connor
content:
Bill Maher complained about the reaction to Dolly Parton’s death, aged 80, during a monologue on his show Real Time.
The comedian and talk-show host began the episode on Friday (28 August) by discussing current events, in particular the United State’s trade war with Canada.
“All this is going on, and all America could really talk about this week was how sad it is we lost Dolly Parton,” he said in a clip shared to X on Friday night.
Parton died on 25 August following a “brief battle” with cancer, her family announced this week.
News of her death has prompted an outpouring of grief and tributes from around the world, as fans remember her musical legacy but also her many acts of generosity, from supporting LGBT+ charities and medical research programmes to donating millions to children’s literacy.
Stars including her goddaughter Miley Cyrus, pop stars Taylor Swift, Beyonce and Sabrina Carpenter, US president Donald Trump and former president Barack Obama have been among those to pay tribute.
![Bill Maher complained about the coverage of Dolly Parton’s death](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/02/07/16/02/Real-Time-with-Bill-Maher.png)
“Everyone around the country, even around the world,” has been honouring Parton, Maher said, throwing in an obvious joke about the singer’s famous chest.
“London, they’re doing things. The Santa Monica ferris wheel is lit up with hearts. The Empire State Building was put up in pink. The Sphere in Las Vegas added a nipple.”
The media has also been extensively covering the US’s trade war with Canada, including Trump’s signed order directing the federal government to call New York’s Lake Ontario “Lake America”.
The two countries have been exchanging retaliatory measures over failed trade negotiations, with Trump reportedly considering additional tariffs or other actions in response to Canada taxing approximately $20bn in American products.
Maher follows Ricky Schroder as one of the few figures to cast a sour note on the response to Parton’s death.
![Country superstar Dolly Parton died this week aged 80](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/28/21/356dc741b52e9858c6ffcacb7b9ea951Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg4MDMxNTAw-2.20308097.jpg)
Schroder, who played Parton’s father, Robert Lee Parton, in two biopic films based on her childhood, said he loved the “9-5” star in spite of “her advocating for Transgender & Covid Vaccine support”.
Fox Sports South Florida co-host Josh Cohen wrote in response to Schroder’s post on X: “Congratulations to former child TV actor Ricky Schroder on becoming the first person to disrespect Dolly Parton in her passing. What an absolute douche.”
Elsewhere, Parton’s music has returned to the Official Singles Chart in the UK following her death, including her hit single “Jolene”, at number nine, and “9-5” at number 12.
Close behind is “Islands In The Stream”, Parton’s 1983 duet with Kenny Rogers at number 13, with consumption up 276 per cent week-on-week.
summary: During a monologue on his show Real Time, comedian Bill Maher complained about the widespread national and global focus on the death of Dolly Parton at age 80. Parton passed away following a brief battle with cancer, prompting international tributes and an outpouring of grief from fans, politicians, and celebrities. Maher, alongside Ricky Schroder, was among the few to cast a sour note on the response to her passing amid ongoing news coverage of a US-Canada trade war.
key_points: Dolly Parton died at age 80 following a brief battle with cancer.
Bill Maher complained during his show about the heavy public and media focus on Parton's death.
Global tributes poured in from fans, celebrities, and politicians following her passing.
Several of Parton's classic hits, including 'Jolene' and '9-5', re-entered the UK Official Singles Chart after her death.

title: I'm A Celebrity's GK Barry reveals harrowing rape ordeal for first time
author: Emily Bashforth
content:
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/comp-1788036935.png?w=646) 
TV star and influencer GK Barry has opened up about being raped aged 17 by an older boss.
The TikTok sensation, who rose to online fame during the pandemic, is known for her sarcastic, dry humour and hilarious stories.
However, behind the hilarious podcast host persona is a trauma she’s never shared until now.
GK, real name Grace Keeling, 27, has spoken out about her sexual assault to send an important message to other women, particularly her young audience, saying it’ll be ‘worth it’ if it helps ‘even one of them’.
The I’m A Celebrity campmate had previously told just five people, including her parents and girlfriend, what she went through and vowed to move on, pretending it didn’t happen.
Get personalised updates on I'm A Celeb
Wake up to find news on your TV shows in your inbox every morning with Metro’s TV Newsletter.
Sign up to our newsletter and then select your show in the link we’ll send you so we can get TV news tailored to you.
Now, in an interview with Fabulous magazine, Grace has explained that she decided to write about the harrowing experience in her new book, It’s Giving Life.
![File photo dated 20/10/25 of GK Barry attending the Pride of Britain Awards at the Grosvenor House Hotel, London. Social media star GK Barry has said she was raped when she was 17. The 27-year-old media personality, whose real name is Grace Keeling, said in a post shared on Saturday that she felt unable to talk about the assault out of fear. Issue date: Saturday August 29, 2026. PA Photo. Photo credit should read: Ian West/PA Wire](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309959979-155c-e1788036975914.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
The social media personality said: ‘I always thought rape was someone in a dark alleyway jumping out at you – but it wasn’t like that at all.’
She recalled that the rape happened during her second year of college during her work experience, with the manager she was reporting to (who was 10 years her senior) once offering to drive her in when she couldn’t get a lift.
Grace pens in her book that he kept ‘touching [her] leg’ and making her ‘uncomfortable’, noting that there was a major ‘power imbalance’ and she didn’t feel able to ask him to stop.
Instead of taking her to the office, he drove them to an empty park, where he demanded she give him oral sex.
‘I didn’t know what else to do except go along with what he was telling me. Resisting or fighting back felt like it might make things worse,’ she said.
‘There was never a moment in my mind where I thought I could say no to what was happening. I was only 17 and scared. I wasn’t able to process the situation and think logically.’
![Editorial use only Mandatory Credit: Photo by Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock (16733315b) Kaye Adams, GK Barry, Katie Piper, Jane Moore 'Loose Women' TV show, London, UK - 06 Mar 2026](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_288113991-afe5.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Grace continued her work experience, fearful that quitting would mean she wouldn’t get into university after failing her course.
Then, on her final day, the then-teenager was taken to a room by her manager, who had already told everyone else to go home.
He locked the door and told her to remove her jeans, assaulting her and leaving her bleeding and in pain.
‘Rape. It’s taken me 10 years to realise that’s what it was.’
Grace ‘blamed [herself]’ after the attack and had found it ‘flattering’ that the ‘good-looking guy’ was giving her attention.
‘I kept thinking, “I should have said no firmer”,’ she said.
![I'm A Celebrity's GK Barry suffers nightmare during hospital dash to A&E](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_234350606-9399.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
‘It was make-or-break for me going to uni, which at that age felt like a huge deal. I thought, “I just will never tell anyone about this”.’
Over time, Grace has been able to ‘come to terms’ with the fact that it ‘shouldn’t have happened’.
She also felt compelled to speak out a year later when she learnt that another girl from her college was going to the same place for work experience, certain that it would ‘happen to her’ too.
Though she found it more traumatic having to ‘relive it’ 12 months on when a teacher was informed.
Due to her age, the college had to tell her parents, and then they reported the rape to the police.
Grace can still ‘remember so clearly’ the moment she had to tell her mum, who was ‘in shock’ but ‘didn’t blame’ her daughter. She then told Grace’s dad, but ‘to this day’, Grace herself has never spoken to him about it directly.
![Editorial Use Only Mandatory Credit: Photo by James Gourley/ITV/Shutterstock (14978441ag) GK Barry is evicted from camp 'I'm a Celebrity...Get Me Out of Here!' TV show, Series 24, Australia - 06 Dec 2024](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_232235573-9688.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Sadly, a few days later when she spoke to a female police officer, she was told that there was ‘very little point’ taking matters further due to a lack of ‘evidence’.
The officer told Grace it was her word ‘against his’, and since she had been texting the man, it was likely to appear ‘black-and-white’, making it harder to secure a conviction.
While Grace ‘understood what she was saying’, she was never reassured.
‘At no point did she say that he had done anything wrong.’
Grace wasn’t offered any further support, she says a decade later, nor did she seek therapy to process the horrific incident.
Still, she has found it ‘helpful’ to open up, particularly to her partner of two years, footballer Ella Rutherford, 26, who responded by telling her the rape was ‘not [her] fault’.
What to do if you've been raped
If you have been the victim of rape, either recently or historically, and are looking for help, support is out there.
- If you have recently been raped and you are still at risk, ring 999 and ask for the police. Otherwise, the first step is to go somewhere you are safe.
- If you want to report your rape to the police, ring 999 or the police non-emergency line on 101. An Independent Sexual Violence Advocate (ISVA) will often be on hand to help you through reporting and even after you have made a statement, you can still decide to withdraw from the criminal justice process at any time.
- If you plan on going to the police, if possible, do not wash your clothes or shower, bathe or brush your teeth. If you do get changed, keep the clothes you were wearing in a plastic bag. These steps will help to preserve any DNA evidence your attacker may have left on your body or clothes.
- If you don’t want to contact the police, Rape Crisis suggest talking to someone you trust about what has happened; or you can ring one of the UK’s many rape and sexual assault helplines.
- Anyone aged 16+ can contact Rape Crisis's 24/7 Support Line by calling 0808 500 2222 or starting an online chat.
- If you have been injured, you’re best advised to go to your nearest A&E to seek medical treatment. If you are uninjured, you can go to your nearest Sexual Assault Referral Centre (SARC). The NHS has information on where to find your nearest centre here.
- If your rape is historic, you can still access support, including from the police – there is no time limit on reporting and your account can still be used as evidence.
Read more here.
‘I think the perception is that rapists are creepy men lurking in the dark, but actually most rapes happen with people you know or are friends with, and that makes it so much harder,’ Grace concluded in the interview.

She shared the harrowing experience in her new book, It's Giving Life, in order to send an important message to other women and her young audience. Although she initially kept the assault a secret and blamed herself, the incident eventually came to light a year later when a teacher was informed to protect another student.

title: Funeral home shares Dolly Parton obituary as family gathers at burial site
author: Asyia Iftikhar; Dolly Parton
content:
![Dolly Parton smiling at an event.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309741578-bf9e.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
A Nashville funeral home has paid tribute to Dolly Parton’s ‘rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see’.
The late country music legend died aged 80 after a ‘brief battle’ with cancer, with celebrities, politicians and influential figures from across the globe honouring her mammoth legacy.
On Friday, close family was seen arriving at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Nashville, where her late husband Carl Dean has already been laid to rest when he died aged 82 in March 2025. She is set to be buried by his side.
The husband-and-wife were together for 59 years after meeting outside a laundrette on the very same day she had moved to Tennessee to pursue her singing career.
They kept their home life to themselves, with Dean only making a few public appearances over the years.
As for Parton, the funeral home shared a sweet message on their site, remembering her life, echoing the initial statement released by the Jolene singer’s representatives.
![Dolly Parton's burial site at Woodlawn-Roesch-Patton Funeral Home & Woodlawn Memorial Park.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309826890-aa33.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
![Dolly Parton's burial site at Woodlawn-Roesch-Patton Funeral Home & Woodlawn Memorial Park.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309826895-2b43.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Hailing her as a ‘global icon and humanitarian’, the obituary continued: ‘Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family.’
Calling her legacy ‘one of love, kindness, and resilience’, they noted that her seven-decade career has inspired ‘multiple generations’.
‘Her songs will continue to resonate with people of all ages, and her philanthropic work will have a lasting impact,’ the familiar statement concluded.
One of the tombstones dedicated to the couple shows their names engraved on top of a scene of the rolling countryside Parton loved so much. Her in-laws are also buried in the same location.
![Dolly Parton](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309751170-160a-e1788012506939.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646)

title: Nepo babies take over music festivals
author: Patrick Sawer
content:
![David and Victoria Beckham look on at Reading where their son Cruz is performing](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000499952485_17880209279860_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqn2n2hk5qKEJ--A9z8HbLAvipp6I7Wmq8QJJkq5qiFBM.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![David and Victoria Beckham look on at Reading where their son Cruz is performing](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000499952485_17880209279860_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqn2n2hk5qKEJ--A9z8HbLAvipp6I7Wmq8QJJkq5qiFBM.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
It’s a long-held music industry adage that old rockers never die, they just fade away.
But now it seems that they are simply being replaced onstage by their offspring.
This weekend, the children of some of the biggest names in rock are performing at the Reading and Leeds Festivals. The big surnames include Gallagher, Grohl and Martin, and a Beckham – even if he’s not strictly the scion of a rock star.
Gene Gallagher, Moses Martin, Violet Grohl and Cruz Beckham will all be taking to the stage as they follow in the footsteps of their parents.
![Cruz Beckham is performing with his band, The Breakers](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000499957783_17880214516470_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqntSheJW8V0esC6Auk1dHGXdR78eTBj0hwdfFRfV9oOU.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Liam Gallagher’s 25-year-old son, Gene, played with his band Villanelle at Reading on Friday and again at Leeds on Saturday. The band, which has been performing since 2024, released its debut single, Hinge, last year, with Gene as lead singer and guitarist.
Moses Martin, the 20-year-old son of Coldplay frontman Chris Martin and his actress ex-wife Gwyneth Paltrow, was playing at both sites with his band, People I’ve Met. The trio released their debut single, Promise, in December 2025.
![Moses Martin](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000499839206_17880126193020_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqxAHgvSpW8b5g6-J_2-NZhnwSCF1R0VweJ7DS2UnVMSQ.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Dave Grohl’s daughter, Violet, who has followed her Foo Fighters frontman father into the music industry, released her debut album, Be Sweet To Me, in May and was also due to perform at both festivals.
![Violet Grohl performs during the 2026 Leeds Festival](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000499846576_17880125933580_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq5_zV_kf2t_tp9pIkAYr4xTiBRKvY0sJuGt5DVbjqiS0.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Cruz Beckham, the son of Spice Girl Lady Victoria and former England football captain Sir David, was performing at Reading with his band, The Breakers, and then at Leeds.
Gene Gallagher has previously spoken about the “nepo baby” label, telling The Sunday Times: “People say to me, ‘Ooh it must be so easy for you to get a band together.’ It’s not. We’re earning our stripes.”
His uncle, Noel Gallagher, has previously said it’s “not healthy” to give children a leg-up – unless they actually have some talent.
![Musician Dave Grohl and daughter Violet in 2011](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000495099841_17880126190072_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqDK2Bw6bdVSq8JHSn5_s4N0IkTzSVQDzCWBheEXvsUzU.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Speaking to the Radio X Evening Show at the time that his daughter, Anais, was starting out as a model and photographer, the Oasis co-founder said: “The whole nepotism thing, I mean it’s human nature to help your children out.
“She’s good at what she does, her photographs are really, really good, and if she was terrible, I wouldn’t be doing it for the sake of it, because I think if you’re knowingly just giving your kids something to do and they’re not really good at it, I don’t think that’s very healthy.”
![Gene Gallagher](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000499856949_17880126192803_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq8BGcGB0fWPmYiKUNlQpYc11cOMOAdwrpi1tLWNmrB9s.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
While the families of nepo rockers say their offspring deserve their place on the bill on merit, others within the music industry have questioned whether they have what it takes.
Nick Grimshaw, the BBC Radio 6 Music presenter, said: “Nepotism goes a long way. You can still make good music.
“But can you make great music? Can you have the same hunger for it?”
summary: Children of prominent music and celebrity figures, including the offspring of members from Oasis, Coldplay, and the Foo Fighters, are increasingly performing at major music events like the Reading and Leeds Festivals. While some family members argue they are earning their place on merit, industry figures and relatives debate whether nepotism grants an unfair advantage or affects artistic hunger. Despite the discussion, these young artists continue to release music and secure festival slots.
key_points: Gene Gallagher, Moses Martin, Violet Grohl, and Cruz Beckham are performing at the Reading and Leeds Festivals.
Gene Gallagher plays in the band Villanelle, Moses Martin is in People I’ve Met, Violet Grohl released a debut album, and Cruz Beckham performs with The Breakers.
Gene Gallagher has pushed back against the 'nepo baby' label, stating that they are earning their stripes.
Noel Gallagher has expressed that giving children a leg-up is only healthy if the children possess actual talent.

title: Tom Cruise's 'Days of Thunder' Sequel Adds Anne Hathaway To Cast
author: Justin Kroll
content:
![](https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/days-of-thunder.jpeg?w=681&h=383&crop=1) 
Paramount Pictures is really revving its engines on the upcoming Days of Thunder 2 starring Tom Cruise, with Anne Hathaway now set to join Cruise in the sequel. Cruise revealed the news Saturday on his social platforms featuring a picture of the two A-listers leaning against a NASCAR race car in Daytona.
The post also announced that the film would be released June 2, 2028. The movie will be filmed for Imax and also available in Dolby cinemas, 4DX and premium large-screen formats.
Hathaway’s addition comes after Paramount tapped Jonathan Levine to direct, hence fast-tracking the pic as Cruise’s next project. Cruise returns as NASCAR driver Cole Trickle, reprising the role from his 1990 hit racing pic. While plot details are unknown, Hathaway is expected to play a team owner and engineer in the follow-up.
Cruise is also producing alongside Jerry Bruckheimer and Tommy Harper. Will Staples penned the script.
Watch on Deadline
Days of Thunder, directed by the late Tony Scott, was released during the summer of 1990 and made $82.6 million at the domestic box office, and $157.9M worldwide. Cruise played Cole Trickle in the Robert Towne-written pic, a hot-headed rookie stock car driver who joins NASCAR and must overcome personal and professional challenges to achieve success. The film also saw him introduced to Nicole Kidman, who became his wife of 11 years, and who went on to star with him in Ron Howard’s Far and Away and Stanley Kubrick’s Eyes Wide Shut.
Cruise conceived the story for the racing movie,which was produced by Don Simpson and Bruckheimer. Robert Duvall, Randy Quaid, Cary Elwes, Caroline Williams and Michael Rooker also starred in the original.
As for Hathaway, she is coming off a big summer that included The Devil Wears Prada 2, The Odyssey and The End of Oak Street. She can be seen next in Verity, which bows in October. She is repped by CAA and Entertainment 360.
summary: Anne Hathaway has joined the cast of Paramount Pictures' upcoming "Days of Thunder 2," starring alongside Tom Cruise, who is reprising his role as NASCAR driver Cole Trickle. Cruise announced the news and a release date of June 2, 2028, on his social media platforms. Jonathan Levine will direct the film, with Hathaway expected to play a team owner and engineer.
key_points: Anne Hathaway has joined Tom Cruise in the cast of "Days of Thunder 2."
The sequel is scheduled for release on June 2, 2028.
Jonathan Levine will direct the film, which will be filmed for IMAX and other premium formats.
Tom Cruise is returning to his role as NASCAR driver Cole Trickle from the 1990 original.
Hathaway is expected to portray a team owner and engineer in the movie.

title: Charli XCX electrifies Reading Festival with era-spanning set
author: Naomi Clarke
content:
![A black and white photo of Charli XCX leaning against a wall as she sings into a microphone. There is a bright white wall behind her which silhouettes her body.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/86ea/live/35df52c0-a32d-11f1-8e46-c39d9fc92d9e.jpg)
The British singer treated fans to hits from her latest albums and her back catalogue
- Published
Charli XCX has ushered in her next era with an electrifying headline set at Reading Festival which showcased hits from across her music career.
It marked the British singer's first UK festival performance since releasing her latest studio album - Music, Fashion, Film - which is a pivot from her culture-shaping, electronic-pop record Brat and features more of a rock edge.
But her Friday evening show highlighted the best of both, alongside fan favourite tracks from her back catalogue.
She also upped the production from her last Brat tour, with more elaborate staging, numerous costume changes, dramatic pyro and strobe lighting, and she was accompanied by a host of dancers and a live band.
![A black and white photo of Charli XCX as she stands on stage surrounded by dancers.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/5f5f/live/9eb4f070-a32d-11f1-8e46-c39d9fc92d9e.jpg)
Distorted, black-and-white videos of Charli kicked off the performance and featured throughout
Distorted, black-and-white videos of Charli kicked off the performance and the tens of thousands who had gathered at the main stage erupted as the chords were struck up to her new album's lead single, Rock Music.
After delivering punchy renditions of new tracks Wink Wink, Yeah and Card Declined, she stepped out to change from a black sparkly blazer into a black corseted dress.
The second act of the performance showcased the breadth of her work, as she moved from pop hit Track 10 from her 2017 mixtape, to the melancholic tones of House, which she co-wrote for the recent Wuthering Heights soundtrack album.
Those still craving her infectious dance tracks welcomed the singer later breaking out songs like Club Classics, 365 and the Grammy-winning Von Dutch from her sixth album Brat, which became a cultural phenomenon and propelled her to new heights in 2024.
After returning to the more punk style of Music, Fashion, Film, she closed with its last track, No One Lasts Forever.
The song concludes with filmmaker David Cronenberg saying "no one lasts forever / they are dead, they are gone" and "oblivion is freedom" - and Charli let that be the last words which rang out as she stared out across the crowd, surrounded by her dancers.
![Skepta performs on stage wearing a green jacket, black gloves and black trousers.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/1da7/live/4a746f40-a328-11f1-8e46-c39d9fc92d9e.jpg)
Skepta powered through the downpours to hype up the main stage crowd before Charli XCX
The rock energy continued on the main stage as Fontaines DC followed Charli, with both acts billed as headliners for the opening night of Reading.
Fans had to wait about half an hour longer due to a delay, but the Irish rock band from Dublin soon won them back around as they launched into hits like Favourite and I Love You.
They closed out the set with their Grammy-nominated track Starbuster from their fourth album, Romance, with the crowd responding by chanting the lyrics back to them.
Ahead of Charli's set, grime artist Skepta also channelled some Brat energy when he took to the main stage in a lime green waterproof jacket as he powered through the downpours to hype up the crowd.
The rapper belting out "it rains, it pours" from his hit collaboration track, Praise the Lord (Da Shine), with A$AP Rocky was particularly fitting, and he ended the set on a high as the crowd jumped along to Victory Lap, his collaboration with Fred Again.. and PlaqueBoyMax.
The rainstorms drew more festival-goers into the new Gallery tent, but US rock band Geese had already pulled in a huge crowd who jumped and head-banged along to guitar-heavy tracks like Half Real and 100 Horses.
Earlier in the afternoon, BBC Radio 1's Sound of 2026 winner Skye Newman's powerful, husky vocals reverberated through the same tent as she performed hit songs like FU & UF and Family Matters.
![Skye Newman sings into a microphone as she performs on stage. She wears a denim top and skirt outfit.  There is a band behind her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/f632/live/97d102c0-a329-11f1-8e46-c39d9fc92d9e.jpg)
Rising star Skye Newman delivered powerful vocals in the new Gallery tent
Jamie T kicked off the main stage at midday after posting a video the day before asking if he could get a "last minute" set, and he used his 33 minutes and 10 seconds, a nod to his new single 3310, to crack out some of his indie hits, including Zombie and Sticks N Stones.
The twin festivals will feature six major headliners this weekend, with bosses previously saying Reading and Leeds will be the only UK festival appearances for all of them this year.
Rapper Dave, singer-songwriter Raye, electronic duo Chase & Status and band Florence + The Machine are all set to top the bill.
![A footer logo for BBC Newsbeat. It has the BBC logo and the word Newsbeat in white over a colorful background of violet, purple and orange shapes. At the bottom a black square reading "Listen on Sounds" is visible.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/e185/live/c8857230-14f0-11ef-976f-87c9f89e656e.jpg)
  - Published1 day ago
 ![Crowds of festival-goers wave their hands in the air at Leeds Festival. There a few people in the crowd raised up by sitting on the shoulders of other people.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/5d84/live/c30d5820-a249-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
- ![Ed Sheeran performs on the BBC Introducing Stage at Reading Festival, 2011. He has bright ginger hair and is wearing a maroon zip-up hoodie. He is singing into a microphone on a stand whilst playing an acoustic guitar.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/7ada/live/ddcf1b50-846f-11f1-b286-f1d324aa6c22.jpg)
- ![Charli XCX - close up of her face and long, dark hair](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b583/live/d382c430-86ae-11f1-8e17-395fea5a1d61.jpg)
summary: British singer Charli XCX delivered an electrifying headline performance at Reading Festival, showcasing music from her new rock-edged album, Music, Fashion, Film, alongside hits from her electronic-pop record Brat and older back catalogue. The elaborate set featured dancers, a live band, costume changes, pyro, and strobe lighting. Other opening-night highlights included sets from Fontaines DC, Skepta, Geese, Skye Newman, and Jamie T.
key_points: Charli XCX's headline performance marked her first UK festival appearance since releasing her new album, Music, Fashion, Film.
The set combined tracks from her new rock-influenced era with fan favorites from her cultural phenomenon album, Brat.
Her performance featured high-production elements including elaborate staging, numerous costume changes, dramatic pyro, strobe lighting, dancers, and a live band.
Other main stage acts on the opening night included Fontaines DC, Skepta, and Jamie T, who filled a last-minute slot.
Performances by artists like Skye Newman and Geese drew large crowds into the new Gallery tent during rainstorms.

title: ‘In walked this big bundle of energy’: the day Dolly Parton came to Rotherham
author: Esther Addley
content:
Shane Jarman was up a ladder decorating a Christmas tree at the school where he was deputy headteacher when he got a call asking him to come to Rotherham hospital ASAP. It was December 2007 and Jarman’s wife, Claire, had given birth the previous day to their first child, a girl called Emma, so of course he rushed to the phone. All was well, he was told, but that “everything would become clear” when he got to the hospital.
Once there, his wife told him – somewhat unexpectedly – that they were going to meet Dolly Parton. “And literally within what felt like five minutes,” he recalled, “there were great camera flashes, lots of noise, lots of clicking and in walked this real big bundle of energy.”
![Dolly Parton holds newborn Emma wrapped in pink, beside her seated parents](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6e57bb0a467e6bc7f6569610eae4484315175923/0_290_1371_771/master/1371.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Jarman said that as his wife handed over their tiny 4lb 6oz baby to the country star, “all I remember is seeing Dolly Parton with my little girl’s head in her hand and these great big red nails”.
Was he a little nervous about the nails? “I was very nervous about the nails to be quite honest.”
Parton was in the South Yorkshire former mining and steelworking town – not principally known for its razzle-dazzle – for the British launch of the Imagination Library, the book donation programme the musician had started in her Tennessee home of Sevier County a little over a decade earlier, and which she had been invited to extend to children in Yorkshire.
![Dolly Parton in green sequinned jacket plays the guitar and sings into a mic](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5dc125dd0d4a7b2d1908e4ca0dfc6dc85e4e206c/0_0_2929_4096/master/2929.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
If Rotherham – or at least a gathering of local dignitaries that assembled later in a disused steelworks – was a little bemused by the singer, Parton knew places like this, and of course knew how to charm.
“I gotta make sure I say your town name right – it’s Rother’m?” she said, flattening the famous southern twang to something approximating flat Yorkshire vowels. “Did I get it right? I’ve been practising because it don’t look like that on paper. In the States, anything that’s h-a-m we have to say Rother-ham.”
Among the torrent of tributes to the entertainer, businesswoman and philanthropist since her death on Monday, Rotherham too has been remembering the impact of a woman who, for all her own glamour, cared deeply about places that had a little less of it.
Parton may have jested when she said she had considered buying a South Yorkshire pied-à-terre (“so you may be walking down the streets of Rotherham and see me coming out of a little cubbyhole somewhere”), but her description of the post-industrialist town as “a heart spot for me” was sincere, thanks to the similarities she saw to her own outsider upbringing.
“I totally related to Rotherham,” she said some years later. “I know that it’s out in an industrial area … When they were making fun of me for going out there, I thought, you know what? Don’t make fun of me.”
The scheme ensured that every child in Rotherham was posted a free book, in their own name, for each month of their life until they were five, funded partly by Parton’s foundation and partly by the local authority and other local funders. Deborah Bullivant, who took over leading the Rotherham Imagination Library shortly after Parton’s visit as part of a wider literacy drive, said that despite some initial scepticism from locals, it “changed the culture” for many.
![Dolly Parton meets young children](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/671e3bc85c2c23f6f3c9c02a936dadf32dcf47d5/0_27_3000_2185/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“Some people were very suspicious: Why Dolly Parton? What is this thing?” she said. “[But] can you imagine receiving a book, from registering your child’s birth, your baby in their own name receives the book every month through the letterbox? For many families who didn’t really have a background in reading, it changed the culture within their homes to being more of a reading culture and embracing books and using books and sharing books.”
The fact that the literacy drive was so personal to the singer was “the best way to counter any of the suspicion or worries that people had about it”, Bullivant said. “Why is Dolly Parton doing this? Who is she? She doesn’t know about this? Well, she does. She understood she needed to drive her own work herself from scratch. She got the importance of the imagination, of reading, of telling stories.”
Though the Rotherham scheme was wound up in 2015 after the council withdrew support, it would be rolled out to other places in Britain, including Doncaster, North Lincolnshire, the London borough of Southwark (“Hello Suth’rk! This is Dolly!”) and Nottingham (which even coaxed an “Ay up me duck!” from the singer).
![Shane Jarman and daughter Emma today.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ac402e43d6ca4ff3a0ece8724ddacc899df2cdc5/0_101_1599_1099/master/1599.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In total, 6.3m books have been given to children across the four UK nations since one-day-old Emma Jarman received the first one in 2007, a copy of The Tale of Peter Rabbit, which Parton autographed for her. (Globally, the figure is 300m).
Emma, now 18, will shortly be going to university to study biomedical science, “and, if I know Emma, [the book] will go to university with her so that she can show her friends there,” said her father.
summary: In December 2007, country star Dolly Parton visited Rotherham hospital to mark the British launch of her Imagination Library book donation programme. There, she met newborn Emma Jarman and presented her with the UK's very first free book under the scheme. Despite initial local skepticism, the literacy drive successfully posted free monthly books to children in the town until council support ended in 2015.
key_points: Dolly Parton visited Rotherham in December 2007 to launch the UK branch of her Imagination Library literacy programme.
Newborn Emma Jarman was the first child in the UK to receive a free book through the scheme, a signed copy of The Tale of Peter Rabbit.
The programme provided free monthly books to children under five, changing reading cultures in homes despite initial local suspicion.
Although the Rotherham scheme ended in 2015, the Imagination Library expanded to other UK areas, contributing to millions of books distributed nationally.

title: Magic carpet: Bayeux Tapestry could fly back to France
author: Craig Simpson
content:
![Bayeux Tapestry](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/28/TELEMMGLPICT000437778782_17879390560010_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Bayeux Tapestry](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/28/TELEMMGLPICT000437778782_17879390560010_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
It took 900 years and an overnight journey for the Bayeux Tapestry to finally cross the Channel, but the return leg could take just under an hour.
The medieval artwork could be flown back to France after its appearance in Britain, the first since it was created here in the 11th century.
The Telegraph understands that “all options are on the table” for its return to Bayeux, including alternative modes of transport.
In July, the 1,000-year-old artwork was taken by road under heavy police escort from the French town to the British Museum, where it will be displayed in a public exhibition.
However, security concerns could prompt planners to choose a new method for returning the artefact.
New and effective shock-proof transport equipment could also allow other routes to be chosen, without risk of damaging the fragile artwork.
Should conservation experts sign off on an aerial route, flights from London to Normandy could take under an hour, and bypass a number of risks on the road itinerary – including potholes.
![The Bayeux Tapestry arrives at the British Museum in the dead of night, July 10](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/28/TELEMMGLPICT000496034683_17879409731190_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Formal planning for the return leg has not yet begun, but it is understood that all possible safe routes, from which authorities can choose, have been tested in advance.
All transport options will remain a closely guarded secret for obvious security reasons – the artwork, detailing William the Conqueror’s victory against King Harold, has been insured by the UK Government for £800m.
Building up to the initial transportation in July, authorities in France and the UK took great pains to remove the risk of attacks or protests targeting the Tapestry while it was on the road.
It is possible that British and French authorities, in the end, will simply choose alternative road routes for the legs either side of the Channel crossing.
Emmanuel Macron, the French president, has taken no chances with the safety of the Tapestry since announcing its historic, and initially controversial, loan in 2025.
Heritage experts raised concerns that the extremely delicate fabric of the 230ft-long artwork would not survive transportation, as the vibration of road travel would shake it apart.
Months of preparation began, and French company Science and Mechanics in Conservation of Heritage was commissioned by France’s culture ministry to package the artwork for its journey.
![Catherine Pégard (centre), the French culture minister looks at the Bayeux Tapestry after its arrival in London](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/28/TELEMMGLPICT000496034670_17879409716761_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
A shock-proof crate was created into which the artwork could be painstakingly “folded” – actually gently bent into 27 sections as folds would break it – and packed between frictionless fabric.
Hizkia, an art transport company, tested a specialist lorry capable of moving the crate in a “cradle”, which effectively absorbed all vibrations caused by driving.
The crate and lorry were taken on to dry runs from Bayeux to London, and the actual move was signed off after the vibration measurement, from these trips was found to be satisfactory.
The vibration mitigation proved so successful that Tapestry suffered the same level of movement, effectively none, that would face by simply hanging in a museum.
While this level of mitigation may allow scope for other modes of transport, sea and air routes were dismissed early on when plans were being drawn up for the first journey across the Channel.
For now, the artwork is safely displayed in the British Museum, where it has been laid out flat in an unbroken 230ft line, ready for the opening of what is expected to be a blockbuster exhibition on Sept 10.
Claudia Winkleman has starred as an employee of the British Museum in a trailer for the exhibition, as a new wave of tickets for the landmark event are announced.
![tmg.video.placeholder.alt 6m3Z6nsusqw](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/6m3Z6nsusqw/maxresdefault.jpg) 
Tickets are sold out until December, but additional tickets will go on sale in October for visits between January and March next year.
Winkleman features in the trailer as a new security employee who is faced with the 1066 Norman invasion and Battle of Hastings as the tapestry is brought to life.
The short film features more than 30 historical re-enactors from across the country as it combines live action and visual effects to tell a tale inspired by the tapestry.
![Winkleman tries to control warring troops in the trailer for the exhibition](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/28/TELEMMGLPICT000499837419_17879612044000_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqNUHzxaamNmHDqK-YksWRz2o-yMLyYquKCawpyDOW254.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Winkleman is seen rushing around the British Museum, moving through its popular galleries and exhibitions while passing some of its recognisable objects as she tries to restore order and control the soldiers.
The video ends with Winkleman fleeing the scene as the two armies meet face-to-face in the great court of the museum for a dramatic confrontation.
The Traitors host Winkleman, who is a trustee of the museum, said: “It was an honour to be part of this excellent film.
“We’re so excited about the Bayeux Tapestry coming to the British Museum and for everyone to see the exhibit.”
summary: The Bayeux Tapestry, currently on display at the British Museum for a landmark exhibition, could be flown back to France rather than transported by road. Security concerns, new shock-proof equipment, and the potential to bypass road hazards like potholes have prompted planners to consider alternative transport options for its return journey. The 1,000-year-old, £800m-insured artwork was initially moved to Britain in July using a specialized vibration-absorbing crate and lorry.
key_points: The 230-foot Bayeux Tapestry is currently featured in an exhibition at the British Museum after arriving in London in July.
Planners are considering flying the medieval artwork back to France to bypass road risks such as potholes and security concerns.
The UK Government has insured the historic tapestry for £800m.
Specialized shock-proof crates and transport methods were successfully developed and tested to protect the delicate fabric from vibrations during its initial journey.

title: ‘Zombie’ Ronnie O’Sullivan mural gets a rocket from snooker fans
author: Tim Sigsworth
content:
![Ronnie O'Sullivan](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/28/TELEMMGLPICT000499701111_17879382311860_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqj-j4M0ph6mb-qQkgzL15T3QjZP3btzjdhJO0lVTcsU0.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Ronnie O'Sullivan](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/28/TELEMMGLPICT000499701111_17879382311860_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqj-j4M0ph6mb-qQkgzL15T3QjZP3btzjdhJO0lVTcsU0.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A “zombie-like” mural of Ronnie O’Sullivan, the snooker player, has prompted dismay from residents of Sheffield.
The depiction of the seven-time world champion on the wall of a snooker club in the South Yorkshire city was described as “zombie-like” and “skeletal”.
Shaun Spalding told BBC News that the artwork was “shocking”.
“His eyes are all wrong, his teeth are wrong, it just don’t look like Ronnie,” he said. “It looks like somebody who’s got a skeletal face.”
Frank Short, another resident, added: “The artwork is OK but the eyes are all wrong. It looks like he’s taken something.”
![Ronnie O'Sullivan](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/28/TELEMMGLPICT000499789433_17879383203840_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqA7N2CxnJWnYI3tCbVBgu9T0aesusvN1TE7a0ddd_esI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Chris Ashmore, who painted the mural, hit back at his critics, saying the painting was “unfinished” and that he was only a fortnight into the five-week job.
“I usually use a scissor lift, where you can stand back and see things as a whole, but I couldn’t use it as the land is too uneven,” he said.
“When the scaffolding came down, I came away and boom – it’s gone viral. I saw people saying it looks like Michael Jackson or a zombie. I’ve got thick skin, I’ll be OK, but it didn’t feel fair.”
He added: “It’s not finished, there’s bits of skin tone to do and I’ll finish it off as and when I can.”
Mr Ashmore was commissioned by the Spot On Snooker Club on Langsett Road to paint the mural on one of its walls.
‘The reactions are becoming personal’
Dan Kirkland, the manager of the club, said the mural needed “tweaking”.
“There are parts of the face that need tweaking, particularly around the eye and mouth,” he said.
“Some relatively small changes will make a huge difference, so we’ll arrange whatever access Chris needs.
“What has upset us is seeing some of the reactions becoming personal towards Chris.
“People are absolutely entitled to like or dislike a mural. But having an opinion about a piece of artwork is one thing. Slagging off the person who created it is another.”
Other locals praised the painting as “brilliant” and said it had “brightened” their day.
The mural is the latest in a long line of public art installations that have been criticised, including a statue of Harry Kane which was unveiled in Walthamstow, London, in 2024, and ridiculed for looking nothing like him.
summary: A mural of snooker player Ronnie O'Sullivan painted on a Sheffield snooker club wall drew criticism from residents who described it as "zombie-like" and skeletal. Artist Chris Ashmore defended the artwork by explaining that it is unfinished and that uneven terrain prevented him from properly stepping back to view it. Club manager Dan Kirkland stated the mural needs tweaking around the eyes and mouth, while condemning personal attacks against the artist.
key_points: A mural of seven-time world champion Ronnie O'Sullivan in Sheffield was criticized by locals for looking skeletal and zombie-like.
Artist Chris Ashmore stated that the mural is unfinished, only two weeks into a five-week job, and was complicated by uneven ground.
Spot On Snooker Club manager Dan Kirkland agreed the face needs tweaking but condemned personal abuse directed at the artist.
Some local residents praised the painting as brilliant and said it brightened their day.

title: Richard Osman "can't really talk" about The Thursday Murder Club movie
author: Sam Warner
content:
Richard Osman has admitted he "can't really talk" about The Thursday Murder Club movie. The adaptation of the bestselling author's murder mystery hit Netflix exactly one year ago, with Helen Mirren, Pierce Brosnan, Celia Imrie and Ben Kingsley starring as the central sleuthing team.
The story follows four retirees who band together to solve a murder, and while largely well received, one controversial change was to the character of Bogdan (Henry Lloyd-Hughes). Bogdan is arrested at the end of the film despite getting away and the crime being concealed in the original book.
Addressing the film, Osman told The Times: "I can’t really talk about the film very much. Let’s not let it detain us."
Related: Best streaming services
However, when pushed further on the big change, he added: "It was only one book. The other books I would like to adapt myself."
The author also admitted it was "a lot of fun meeting [Steven] Spielberg, Helen, Pierce and everyone else" and was "really cool".
This isn't the first time Osman has alluded to the Bogdan backlash, sharing last year in a newsletter: "We'll all be aware of some of the 'differences' between the film and the first book (see the title of this newsletter)," accompanied by a "#JusticeForBogdan" hashtag.
Whether The Thursday Murder Club gets a sequel remains to be seen, with the movie attracting solid if not particularly spectacular viewing figures upon its immediate release.
During the new chat, Osman also reflected on the book series' fandom and getting to meet readers, sharing: "No one has ever said, ‘I loved that plot twist,’ or, ‘I loved that sentence.’ They say, ‘Oh, Joyce is just like my mum,’ or, ‘I’m a bit of an Elizabeth,’ or, ‘I’m in love with Bogdan.’ I love that.
"Because of everything I’ve done and will ever do, the books are me, the representation of my heart and my soul. Getting to talk about the books to people — that’s the absolute dream."
The Thursday Murder Club is available to watch now on Netflix.
